# Restoration Monitoring

**Connect restoration, science and experience so a river program can
keep learning across projects and generations.**

Restoring a river is a long endeavor. The questions that motivate a
project, the decisions made during design, the observations collected
years later and the lessons shared among partners may be scattered
across many documents and systems. Making those connections easier to
find and understand can help the people caring for the river build on
the work of those who came before them.

`restorationmonitoring` is an early-stage R package and design
initiative for the Upper Mississippi River Restoration (UMRR) and
Navigation and Ecosystem Sustainability Program (NESP) communities. It
supports development of a science and restoration integration component
for the **Environmental Monitoring and Management Application (EMMA)**.
The initiative draws on the partnership’s established expertise, program
records and information systems.

## A shared foundation for learning

The long-term ambition is to let a practitioner begin with a research
question, study, project or restoration practice and explore the
knowledge connected to it. A report could bring together the history and
scientific context, relevant observations, findings and decisions, while
showing the sources and limitations behind each connection.

This approach is intended to help teams discover useful evidence,
recognize gaps, identify opportunities to learn and carry their
judgments forward as projects and staff change. It is designed to work
with incomplete histories: a documented study can be useful even when
some records were never created or can no longer be found.

EMMA, Restoration Features and UMRR-DB are separate systems. This
project is a development sandbox for a proposed extension of EMMA’s data
model; it draws on read-only imports from the Restoration Features GIS
repository and UMRR-DB, along with research, monitoring sources and
partner knowledge. For design purposes, EMMA is the likely home for
future practitioner-authored findings, assessments and decisions; the
details remain open. See the [system
boundaries](https://github.com/MVR-GIS/restorationmonitoring/blob/main/dev/architecture/relational-model-and-extraction-roadmap.md#system-boundaries-and-data-flow).

## Explore the work

The [Research & Design
guide](https://mvr-gis.github.io/restorationmonitoring/RESEARCH-DESIGN-GUIDE.html)
introduces the developing data model, draft reports, worked examples and
supporting evidence. It links directly to the project’s maintained
research and design records for readers who want to follow the
reasoning.

The project is in conceptual design and early package development. Its
reports use curated examples to test ideas; they are not live searches
across all program holdings or approved project assessments. The current
package provides a Steamboat Island report renderer and summary
function, with other prototypes under development. Partner review,
system integration and production decisions remain ahead.

## Install

Install the development package from GitHub with R:

``` r

install.packages("remotes") # if needed
remotes::install_github("MVR-GIS/restorationmonitoring")
```

Report rendering also requires Pandoc. The package does not include all
external program documents and development inputs used in the examples;
see the [document-processing
workflow](https://github.com/MVR-GIS/restorationmonitoring/blob/main/dev/workflows/document-processing.md)
for the current scope and instructions.

The package is dedicated to the public domain under [CC0
1.0](https://github.com/MVR-GIS/restorationmonitoring/blob/main/LICENSE).
